metadata.title: Claude, Finding It.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: my company already wrote this down somewhere — can Claude just find it? Lands the carry-out that enterprise search gives faster reach over what you can already see, not new access.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B04 (the 'Q3 notes' file hiding a payment-processor decision from filename search)

beats.narration_text: The assumption is that Claude just crawls the whole company. It doesn't — it only reaches what you personally can already open. So the real question: using just your own access, can Claude find what your company already wrote down?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'My company already wrote this down. Can Claude search everywhere for it?', hesitates on 'everywhere', corrects to 'only what I can see'

props.text:
My company already
wrote this down.

everywhere for it?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('everywhere' -> 'only what I can see') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: In any company that's been running a while, the answer usually already exists — buried in someone's doc, a slide deck, a chat thread. The problem isn't creation, it's reach. So the reasonable reaction is: I already searched, it isn't there. Here's what's actually happening: normal search only matches the filename, not the words inside. Name a document "Q3 notes" when it actually holds the reasoning for switching payment processors, and searching "payment processor" returns nothing. The label and the contents have no mechanical link — filename search treats them as unrelated objects.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a file labeled 'Q3 notes' sits dark, a query 'payment processor' sweeps every filename and misses by a mile

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - names lie
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A file card labeled 'Q3 notes' sits on cream. A query bar reading 'payment processor' sweeps across a row of filenames; none of them match, and the Q3-notes card stays dark and unfound. THIS EXACT FILE CARD RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: Enterprise search takes that mismatch apart. It reads the words inside your documents, not the label on the folder — and it fans out across your drive, your wiki, your shared folders, your chat, all in one pass. The design bet: you're better at remembering roughly what something was about than exactly where it lives. So you ask in plain language, the way you'd ask a colleague — no boolean operators, no query syntax. That trades away the precision a power user might want, but wins on the case that actually happens: you remember the topic, not the storage.

shot.new_visual_element: The same 'Q3 notes' file opens; the query lands on a sentence deep inside it; several source streams flow into one simultaneous search

production_viz.label: It reads inside, everywhere at once
production_viz.mechanic: The 'Q3 notes' card opens; a terracotta highlight lands on one sentence buried inside it. Beside it, four labeled streams (drive, wiki, folders, chat) flow inward and converge into a single search bar.

beats.narration_text: It doesn't stop at retrieval. The found document slides into the conversation itself as context. Ask "how did we decide on Stripe over PayPal, and why," and if anyone wrote that reasoning down — even casually, in a meeting note — Claude answers from that document, not from what it generally knows. That's the trade-off exposed: without it, Claude reasons from best practices, the average of everything on the internet. With it, Claude reasons from your own decisions. Same model, different source material, radically different answer. The bet is that grounded-in-your-context beats generic-but-authoritative for most of the work you actually do.

shot.new_visual_element: A found document slides into a conversation panel and becomes context; two answer-arrows, one generic drifting wide, one grounded landing on target

production_viz.label: Grounded, not generic
production_viz.mechanic: A document card slides rightward into a chat panel and merges with it (context injection). Below, two arrows fired at the same target: a pale 'generic best practice' arrow lands wide; a sharp 'grounded in your own decisions' arrow lands on the bullseye.

beats.narration_text: Now the honest part. It searches only what you can already see — your credentials, your permissions, nothing new. So finding that Q3-notes file isn't magic; you could always have opened it yourself. Enterprise search saves you the walk, not the ticket. And the reverse holds: not finding something doesn't mean it isn't written down — it might just not be connected or indexed yet. Which is why it does nothing until you point it at your sources. The first index takes a while, because it actually reads every document you granted access to; after that, searches are fast, because it's querying its own store instead of crawling live. Classic trade — pay the cost once up front, pay almost nothing after.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same 'Q3 notes' file inside a boundary ring labeled 'your existing access'; the search wavefront stops hard at the ring

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - bounded by your access
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 FILE CARD RETURNS, identical, now sitting inside a bright ring labeled 'your existing access'. A search wavefront expands outward from the query bar and stops hard at the ring — it cannot cross. A small connect-then-index note sits beneath: sources flow in, then settle into a fast, queryable store.

beats.narration_text: Enterprise search doesn't give Claude new access — it gives you faster reach over what you can already see, because it reads what's actually written, not just what it's named.

props.quote: Enterprise search doesn't give Claude new access — it gives you faster reach over what you can already see, because it reads what's actually written, not just what it's named.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: Help me set up enterprise search for my team. First, ask me which tools our documents actually live in — drive, wiki, shared folders, chat. Then, based on my answer, tell me the three questions I should try first to prove it works, and one decision I should start documenting this week so it's searchable later. Go deeper: ask the same model what your team is quietly re-deciding right now because the original reasoning was never written down anywhere searchable.
